events.notes: We have found these little guys in and around our trash. One time, one was actually stuck inside a garbage can that had a lid that prevented escape. as I do the trash on Wednesdays with my high school volunteers, it surprised us, but we surprised it more! He (or she) just played dead. we thought he was sick until we learned their behaviors. We ended up just dumping the trash completely in the quiet corner of our park in some ferns so he would be protected. he never moved. Two hours later we checked, he was gone and we cleaned the trash we had left
events.summary: Full page drafted from an empty record. The editor's trash-can encounter is the page's best story and anchors what_it_does_here; the involuntary nature of thanatosis runs as the page's through-line without being repeated word-for-word across sections. The widely circulated 'opossums eat thousands of ticks' claim was intentionally omitted — peer-reviewed field studies of wild opossum stomach contents found no ticks, and the claim originated from captive-animal lab work.

events.notes:
This is a strong draft. The **trash-bin story is exactly the right spine**, and Claude did a good job resisting the tired tick claim. I would keep most of it, but there are several places where it gets too absolute or slips into “sounds true, therefore say it confidently.”

The biggest factual correction is right at the top:

> “The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial native to North America.”

That is too broad because Mexico has other native marsupials. UF/IFAS’s cleaner wording is **“the only marsupial north of Mexico.”** Smithsonian says the same. ([Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS][1])

So I’d use:

> **The Virginia Opossum is the only marsupial native north of Mexico.**

Likewise the teaser should say **“North America’s only marsupial north of Mexico”** or, more naturally:

> **The only native marsupial in the United States and Canada...**

### At a Glance

The first item is excellent once that geography is fixed. I might replace “coma-like” with **“catatonic”** or simply “death-like,” because UF/IFAS specifically describes a catatonic state lasting up to four hours. ([Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS][1])

I’d write:

> **When badly frightened, an opossum may collapse into a death-like state that can last minutes or even hours. It is involuntary — the animal is not deciding to put on an act.**

The newborn paragraph is terrific. Thirteen-day gestation, honeybee-sized young, and thirteen teats are all directly supported by UF/IFAS. ([Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS][1]) Keep it.

The **50 teeth** fact is also excellent and verified. ([Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS][1])

The lifespan fact is good too: Florida guidance gives **1–2 years in the wild**, unusually short for a mammal that size. ([Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS][2])

I might, however, replace the last sentence:

> For an animal that so often appears to be dead, they spend their brief lives moving through a surprising amount of territory.

It feels written rather than observed. Maybe:

> **Wild opossums usually live only
events.summary: Applied all editor corrections: geography fix ('north of Mexico'), weight localized to Florida average, removed false-confidence claims about daylight sightings and collapsed opossums, replaced embellished trash-bin story with editor's retelling, cut rabies paragraph, added venom-resistance fact (confirmed UF/IFAS and peer-reviewed literature), and tightened tone throughout.
